$doc: The negative-test matrix for scripts/check-boundaries.mjs, as data.
Every case is a whole miniature repo: `base` below, plus this case's `files`,
minus its `remove`. The checker is then run against it as a child process, at
arm's length, exactly as CI runs it — no import of its internals, so the thing
under test is the shipped gate rather than a copy of its regexes.
WHY THIS IS JSON AND NOT A .mjs MODULE. The sources below contain deliberate
boundary violations. check-boundaries.mjs scans every .mjs/.js/.cjs/.ts/.tsx
file in the repo and cannot tell a string containing `import "../lib/x.js"`
from an import — so holding these cases in a JavaScript file would fail the
very gate they exist to test. A .json file is not scanned. That is also the
honest shape: this is a table, and it reads as one.
`expect.exit` 1 means the case must FAIL the gate; `expect.exit` 0 means it
must PASS. The passing cases are not filler — a rule that bans css/ or
design-system/ from js/, or that reads a path out of a comment, breaks the
pages and the css gate, and nothing else in the repo would notice.
READ THE apps/next PAIR TOGETHER. `import "../../js/main.js"` appears twice
below, byte for byte: once from apps/next/port.ts, where it escapes to the
repo's js/ and must fail, and once from apps/next/src/app/page.tsx, where it
lands on apps/next/src/js/ — the app's own port directory — and must pass.
The two cases differ only in which file holds the string. That is the whole
argument for resolving a reference before matching it, and neither case means
anything without the other.

base.apps/next/scripts/sync-artifacts.mjs:
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
export const sheet = readFileSync(new URL("../../../css/style.css", import.meta.url), "utf8");
